lesson.title: Keep the rows that answer the question

steps.headline: Comparing a column with a value gives a mask, one True or False per row.

lead.text: df['units'] >= 3 does not pick rows by itself. It gives a Boolean mask with one True or False for each row. df[mask] then keeps only the rows where the mask is True.
Build the mask first. Then use it to select.
The test is applied to each value separately. A value equal to the limit passes a >= test.

reveal.text: You applied the test one value at a time, and the True rows are the ones that survive. The mask keeps every row tied to its own data.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
mask = df['units'] >= 3
result = df[mask]

values.name: mask
values.display:
0    False
1    False
2     True
3     True
Name: units, dtype: bool

steps.headline: Rows are (Bay, 2), (Hill, 6), (Bay, 8) and (Hill, 1). How many pass shop 'Bay' and units above 5?

workedSteps.text: Find the Bay rows first: the first and the third.
Join the two tests with & and put each in brackets.
Among the Bay rows, only the third has more than 5 units.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df[(df['shop'] == 'Bay') & (df['units'] >= 3)]

steps.headline: Rows are (Bay, 2), (Bay, 5) and (Hill, 7). How many pass shop 'Bay' and units above 3?

lead.text: Multiplying two columns gives one value per row. Assigning to a new column name adds that column.

reveal.text: Each row's units multiplied its own price, giving one revenue per row. Summing that column gives the total.

steps.headline: df.loc[mask, column] = value changes the rows you chose, in df itself.

lead.text: A single loc assignment names the rows and the column together, and writes to df. Chained indexing, such as df[mask]['price'] = 6, selects first and assigns second, and may change a temporary object instead.

lead.text: A table has shops Bay, Hill, Bay and Hill, with prices 3, 7, 3 and 7. You run df.loc[df['shop'] == 'Bay', 'price'] = 10.

reveal.text: The mask chose the two Bay rows and the assignment wrote to df directly. Rows the mask left out kept their old prices.

lesson.orientation: Build Boolean masks, derive columns and make explicit assignments.
lesson.reviewLabel: Keep the rows that answer the question
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Four orders came in: Bay 2 units, Hill 1 unit, Bay 3 units and Hill 4 units. Orders of 3 units or more are shipped free.

intro.promise: By the end you'll filter a table with a mask, combine two conditions, and add or change a column on exactly the rows you mean.

recap.keyIdea: A comparison gives a mask, & and | combine masks inside brackets, and loc with a mask changes exactly the rows you chose.

blocks.text: You found that two of the four orders qualify, and that one row passes both tests. After the Bay correction the price column totals 34.

recap.nextHook: Next: keep an unknown value separate from a zero.

questions.prompt: For units 1, 4, 6 and 2, how many rows pass units >= 4?
hints: Evaluate the threshold for each row.
Test >= 4 on each value on its own.
Count the True results, including a value equal to the limit.
questions.onCorrect: 2. The values 4 and 6 pass, and 4 counts because the test is >=.

misconceptions.feedback: The value 4 passes too, because >= includes the limit.
The smallest value fails the test.

questions.prompt: How many rows pass both tests?
hints: Both comparisons must be true for the same row.
Look only at the Bay rows.
Count the ones with units above 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the Bay row with 5 units passes both conditions.

questions.onCorrect: 1. Of the Bay rows, only the one with 5 units also passes the units test.

misconceptions.feedback: Both Bay rows pass the first test, but one has only 2 units.
The Hill row fails the first test.

questions.prompt: Which expression combines two pandas comparisons safely?
hints: Use the elementwise operator and bracket each comparison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Parenthesised comparisons joined by & form an elementwise AND mask.

questions.onCorrect: Brackets round each comparison, joined with &. The word and only works on single True or False values.

misconceptions.feedback: and cannot join two whole columns of True and False. Use & instead.
A single equals sign assigns. It does not compare.

hints: Keep the row and column selection in one assignment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A single loc assignment targets rows and a column on df. Chained indexing can target a separate object.

questions.onCorrect: df.loc[mask, 'price'] = 6. One assignment names the rows and the column, and writes to df.

misconceptions.feedback: That selects first and assigns second, which may change a temporary copy.
print only shows rows. It changes nothing.

questions.prompt: Units are 2 and 3, and prices are 7 and 5. What is the total revenue from units * price?
hints: Multiply matching positions, then add.
Revenue is worked out for each row before summing.
Work out 2 × 7 + 3 × 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row revenues are 14 and 15, totalling 29.

questions.onCorrect: 29. The row revenues are 14 and 15, and their total is 29.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the sums of the columns. Work row by row.

questions.prompt: A five-row DataFrame receives df['fee'] = 3. What is df['fee'].sum()?
hints: The assignment applies to every row.
A single value fills the whole new column.
Add five equal fees.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The single value fills all five rows, and 5 × 3 = 15.

questions.onCorrect: 15. A single value was repeated down all five rows, and the sum adds those repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one fee. The new column holds one in every row.

hints: The mask chooses rows first.
Which units pass >= 4?
Add the units of the chosen rows.
questions.prompt: Units are 1, 4, 6 and 2. What is df.loc[df['units'] >= 4, 'units'].sum()?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The rows with 4 and 6 pass, and 4 + 6 = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10. The mask kept the values 4 and 6, and the sum added only those.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every unit. The mask keeps only the rows that pass.
That counts the rows that pass. The sum adds their units.

hints: Check each order's units against 3.
3 itself counts, because the rule says 3 or more.
Count the orders that pass.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The orders with 3 and 4 units pass.

questions.onCorrect: 2. You tested each order separately and kept the ones that passed. That is what a Boolean mask does.

misconceptions.feedback: The order with exactly 3 units also qualifies, because the rule says 3 or more.
Only the 3-unit and 4-unit orders reach the limit.
